questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I preferred an English speaking country overseas with beautiful nature.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Finding the deadlines was at times difficult, and searching for courses was also a bit complicated.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The international/exchange team were very helpful in answering questions and there was an orientation week for international students where a lot of questions were answered.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: We were a group of five searching for places on airbnb which were available for long term rent, and then we ended up contacting a host and making a contract with him without involving airbnb to save some money – after facetiming with him, seeing the house on FaceTime and seeing his ID!

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It can be difficult at times, since the university (if you find housing on your own) won't necessarily supply a safety net for you like they do if you find housing through them either on or off campus. Although we had several problems, our landlord did the best he could to accommodate us, and I think it definitely helped that we have all been living away from home for many years now, so we know how to handle most situations:-) We definitely saved money on it, but it is also worth noting that if you don't find a group to live with, on-campus housing for sure is the right choice to be able to meet new people!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: A lot of steps and unnecessary stress, and not a lot of autonomy to do things yourself, which made it more time consuming.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: First you had to go to a webpage and apply for confirmation from the faculty that you are eligible to take the course, and after that you have to send a mail to the International Learning Team and ask them to enroll you in the course, if you were accepted to take it.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The International Learning Team – they were quick and helpful, when you contacted them.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Quite succesful, but I also applied for big and broad courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Ask the uni if you need help. It is not worth it trying to figure things out yourself. The mail is goabroad@
uwo.ca
.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Easier or similar to Danish levels depending on the year of the class (i.e. 1000 courses were easy, 3000 were somewhat similar to Danish levels).

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Lecture slides contained a lot more information than back home and there were not any required books in any of my classes – meaning no preparation necessary for class. Exams and midterms were multiple choice or short answers, so you have to know a lot of specific things rather than being able to use an overall knowledge to answer essay  questions. Lastly, our course grades consisted of several components, i.e., quizzes, attendance to tutorial hours (typically a low percentage of the total grade), midterms, and assignments.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
2500A Microbiology and Immunology
3592 Biology – Principles of Human Genetics
1111A Health Sciences – Achieving Balance and Meaning
2020A Psychology – Drugs and Behavior

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
2500A had an interesting immunology unit (about a third of the total course), the parasitology/virology unit was quite interesting, but the exam on this unit was too specific and hard and the same goes for the bacteriology unit. 

3592A was interesting but similar to a course back home in Denmark. The professor Patrick McDonald was very good and invested though, so I didn't mind learning it all again:-)

1111A was very easy and quite interesting, but you were only allowed to miss two tutorial hours without a valid explanation, which sucks a bit since they were not very useful.

2020A was very interesting, but you could only have written or printed notes for the exam and there was a weekly quiz, meaning that you had to watch the 3 hours of lectures (posted online, but 6 hours with comprehensive note taking...) within a week, so not so flexible, but also not possible to fall behind:-) Hated the exam (VERY specific with only hand written notes, so time was wasted flipping through notes to find answers), but thought most content was very interesting. Not too much psychology, mostly facts about different drug classes.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The university health plan (~1500 kr.), which was mandatory although I had an extended travel insurance from home with high coverage

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Almost all food (especially cheese, but also vegetables) and data was way more expensive than expected. Access to the recreation center (gym, pools for swimming, and many other sports) was however included in the price paid to the university (~2500 kr.) which we only thought covered mandatory bus card and health insurance, so that was a pleasant surprise.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It seemed like they had many great clubs for any taste, but with only four months and a lot of trips planned I didn't feel like I had the time for any.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Weekly 'Global Café' for exchange students, free home games for all sports teams (we watched American football and ice hockey), the recreation center as mentioned before was free, homecoming weekend, and a bunch of small initiatives such as therapy dogs you could pet in the exam week etc. which you do however have to look out for on the uni's social medias to find out are there. There is also a café called The Spoke and one called The Grad Club which frequently host events such as trivia night. Lastly you can also attend free student concerts, which is actually a fun opportunity even if you are not typically interested in music at all.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Anything you have the energy for honestly – don't hesitate to do something you would like to try! And go to some of the uni sports games, it is very extravagant and a very different (but fun!) experience than you would ever have back in Denmark. On instagram follow @londonblo.g as they post both news from London and information about upcoming events in town such as Christmas Markets:-) And go watch a hockey game at Budweiser Gardens in London or a baseball game in Roger's Centre in Toronto – but figure out the overall rules beforehand, otherwise it might not be too fun:-)

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Save up money for a loooot of trips! London in itself is not too interesting (but give it a chance hehe), but Canada has so many gorgeous national and provincial parks to visit. Be sure to plan when you want to go where early on, as different times of fall is good for different places. I went to the Thousand Islands area, Banff, Algonquin, and Bruce Peninsula all within a month (late September to late October), but there are many recommendations online as to when you should go where for optimal experiences:-) I also highly recommend traveling in an RV or a camping van if you go to the provincial/national parks (and remember to book camp sites)!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: You have to consider taxes and tips all the time, which is annoying and confusing, and also everything is very big –stores, distances, roads etc., so it's not as charming and cozy as in Denmark.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Local students will typically be younger than you as they start uni, when they're 18 or 19, and many of them just moved away from home, meaning that the majority (at least in my experience) were quite young and immature, so I would actually recommend socializing with other exchange students instead. If you want to meet local students you should just go to one of the many bars/clubs just about any day of the week...:-)

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The taxes and tips, the not so charming mega centres located just about anywhere in Canada, and the fairly high amount of homeless people, who don't seem to receive any help. Also Canadians drive anywhere meaning that supermarkets might be placed out of walking distance from your home making it difficult to do grocery shopping.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Many (especially older) Canadians are very kind and open, and they seem to genuinely care about having a good conversation with you. Also (in London, Ontario at least) almost all people say thank you to the bus driver, when they get off the bus, and I think that is very cute.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Campus is beautiful, and London town might seem a bit rough, but do yourself a favor and look for hiking spots in and around the city, cute cafes or other fun experiences instead of discarding the town too quickly!
2. Maybe I was lucky with my courses, but most aren't TOO hard to pass (and remember your grades won't get transferred), so please don't forget to allow yourself to go on extended weekend trips and skipping a few lectures to get the most out of the unique travel opportunities Canada offers. 
3. Follow a lot of the uni's social media accounts to know, what is happening and when, as they have many events that you won't necessarily know about, if you don't check, what they post.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
As mentioned before, if you have any questions (mainly about academics or your exchange spot), write to goabroad@
uwo.ca
– they're super helpful and sweet!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: All the experiences I got to have with my friends both small everyday things and big trips and getting to meet and talk to people from all over the world – even if I might never see them again.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The time difference – it was sometimes hard planning calls home. And also spending more money than I'm used to without earning any:'-) (but the money spent is worth it!)

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Don't forget that a lot of days are spent doing everyday things such as cleaning, studying, cooking etc. just in another country than Denmark, meaning that not every day is an adventure, and that is totally okay! You can't have non-stop perfect exchange days for four months straight.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
